extracted_by: hand, T-0258 piece 2 — the Democrat read, December 1833 (Vol. I Nos. 2-6)
note: Vol. I No. 3, 1833-12-10 — the densest issue of the month and the best-set. Twelve claims, more than any other December number, because this is where the town's business columns are legible: page 1 column 2 and page 2 column 1 together hold fourteen Chicago advertisements, page 3 columns 5 and 6 hold the December ordinances and four more, and page 4 column 5 reprints the November ordinances clean. FIVE THINGS ENTER THE CORPUS HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE: the county Clerk's office placed off Col. Owen's house (c005), a house on lot 7 block 8 that had been a meeting house (c006), Pierce & Abbott named as the blacksmiths opposite the Chicago Hotel (c007), Hardscrabble placed by its section, township and range (c012), and the Board of Trustees meeting in Dexter Graves's house (c008). THE DIALECT: ruled `===== SOURCE PDF PAGE n / ISSUE PAGE m =====` page banners with `--- Column k ---` rules under them. T-0258 PIECE 2 — DECEMBER 1833, Vol. I Nos. 2-6, five issues, read through. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST STANDS ANYWHERE IN THE MONTH: all five transcriptions were swept for every form the Democrat uses elsewhere — 'list of letters', 'letters remaining', 'remaining in the post office', 'uncalled for', a signature ending 'P. M.' and the bare words 'post office' — for three hits, none of them a list (a Detroit post-office contract and a 'send by the Post-Office at our risk' line on 1833-12-10, and the President's message on the General Post Office Department on 1833-12-31). The epic's ruling 1 is therefore met by demonstrating absence, as T-0261 met it for the American and T-0308 for November; only four of T-0258's thirty issues carry a list and none of them is in December. THE MONTH'S STANDING ADVERTISEMENTS ARE CLAIMED ONCE, AT THEIR BEST-READ PRINTING, NOT FIVE TIMES. Sixteen cards run unchanged across two or more of these issues, and the OCR of each varies wildly from setting to setting; a claim is made in the issue where the line that carries the evidence is legible, and the other settings are named in its note as the cross-check. That is why the per-issue counts are uneven (8/12/7/7/7) and why a card that first appears in Vol. I No. 2 may be claimed from Vol. I No. 3. The alternative — one claim per printing — would have multiplied the same forty-one readings into about ninety and made the gazetteer's first_seen dates no better. THE ESTRAY NOTICES ARE QUARANTINED AND NOT CLAIMED, as T-0308 quarantined them: 'Taken Up' by Harry Boardman on the Du Page, by William See at Walker's Grove and by William Taylor in the county are Cook county filings attested by the Clerk of the Commissioners' Court, not Chicago matter, and the animals and appraisers in them belong to the county's prairie and not to the town. THE DEPOSIT IS ON `main` AND THIS BRANCH IS `dev`, so every quote here was machine-checked with `tools/compile_gazetteer.py --check --deposit <a read-only copy of the deposit from main>` before the PR was opened; on `dev` these claims are counted unresolved and reported, which is green (T-0275).

placement.note: A BLOCK FACE, NOT A POINT. The heading names the two cross streets and not the street the face is on, so this places the store inside one block-long run and no closer. The street is left null here deliberately.

claims.notes: P. PRUYNE & CO. STAND BETWEEN CLARK AND DEARBORN, AND THIS IS THE ONLY PLACEMENT THE FIRM HAS ANYWHERE IN THE CORPUS. Pruyne & Co. appear on 1834-01-21 c004 selling a School Section lot and nothing there says where they trade. Here the heading is a placement of a kind the schema has no better class for than `relative`: not a corner and not a bare street, but a BLOCK FACE — the run between two named cross streets. The street the face belongs to is NOT printed: the reading takes it as South Water because that is where the December advertisers who do name a street stand, and that reasoning is recorded rather than the street being asserted. 1833-12-31 sets the same heading (page 3 column 6, 'STORE BETWERS CLARK AND Deanzons-srnnate') and agrees on the two cross streets, which is what makes the reading of this line safe.

claims.notes: A TAVERN CHANGING HANDS, AND THE PREDECESSOR'S NAME IS SPELT TWO WAYS INSIDE THIS MONTH. This is the succession chain the ticket asks for — 'that noted Tavern Stand … lately occupied by' — and it is the SAME standing card as 1833-11-26 c006, so it is one tavern and not two. What December adds is a disagreement: THIS printing reads the outgoing keeper as 'Mr. Wm. Y. Watts' and 1833-12-31 (page 3 column 4) reads 'Mr. Wm. Y. Wattles' in the same sentence. 1833-11-26 c006 read Wattles and 1834-01-28 c009 names John W. Wattles, so Wattles is the better-attested form and 'Watts' is recorded as this printing's variant rather than as a second man. THE MIDDLE INITIAL IS NOT SETTLED EITHER: this setting reads Y, 1833-12-31 reads a currency sign the segmenter substitutes for a capital, and 1833-11-26 c006 read W. The normalized reading takes W from the November claim rather than minting a third Wattles in the gazetteer on a character the transcription cannot hold, and that choice is a choice, not a reading. THE INCOMING KEEPER'S NAME IS NOT IN THIS SETTING AT ALL — the 'KEPT BY' line is blank in the transcription — and it is claimed instead from 1833-12-31, where it reads as Chester Ingersoll. The dateline Oct. 4, 1833 predates the paper's own first number, so the tavern changed hands before the Democrat existed.

claims.notes: MASON & CO. ON MAIN-STREET, AND THE ANCHOR IS STILL UNRESOLVED. The same card as 1833-11-26 c020, set clean here where that one was broken, and it confirms both halves of the anchor that claim could only half-read: 'on Main-street' and 'nearly opposite Graves' Tavern'. NEITHER IS A FEATURE THIS RECONSTRUCTION HOLDS — the 1830 plat has no Main Street, and no Graves' Tavern stands in the structure data — so the placement is recorded verbatim and mapped onto nothing, exactly as c020 recorded it. What is now certain is that the two words are the paper's and not the segmenter's. Dexter Graves is a real and separately attested man: the Board of Trustees met at his house on 4 December 1833 (c010 of this issue), so a Graves' Tavern in the town is very likely his and this is the nearest the corpus comes to placing it.

Owen, president of the Board of Trustees, who signs the town ordinances two columns away in this same issue (c010, c011). His house is therefore a standing building in the town in December 1833 and is now an anchor two claims deep — which is worth more to the reconstruction than the office itself, because it says a documented dwelling stood next door but one to the county's own room. NEITHER BUILDING IS PLACED ON A STREET by this notice, and none is supplied.

claims.notes: A MEETING HOUSE, A LOT AND BLOCK NUMBER, AND A BRIDGE — three things the reconstruction can use, in one auction notice. The lot is named to the plat ('LOT 7, in block 8'), the building on it is given a FORMER USE ('formerly occupied as a Meeting House') and the pair is placed near the bridge on the North Branch. This is the earliest meeting house in the corpus: the Presbyterian church is not dedicated until January 1834 (1834-01-21 c002) and the Baptist meeting house first appears on 1834-01-28 c003, so a building that had ALREADY ceased to be a meeting house by December 1833 stands before either. THE OCR WILL NOT CARRY THE SENTENCE THAT JOINS THEM: 'and house op, the / 4 formerly occupied as a Meeting House' has lost whatever stood between, so it is possible — not likely, but possible — that the meeting house and the lot are two items in one sale rather than one. That doubt is recorded and not resolved. The auctioneer is James Kinzie.

Be it further Ord[ai]ned by the Board of Trustees of the town of Chicago, That each and every owner o[r] occupant of any lot in said town, fronting upon the Chicago River or its branches, where the street runs to said river, be permitted to occupy the vacant ground on said river, leaving eigh[t]y feet for a street, for wharfing privileges only; And for the purpose of guaran[t]e[e]ing th[is] right, each and every owner o[r] o[c]cupant, desiring such privilege, shall upon paying fifteen [d]ollars annually in advance, to the Treasurer of said Board, be entitled to a lease, for the ter[m] of five years from the first day of J[a]nuary [next,] signed by the President
claims.notes: THE WHARFING ORDINANCE, IN ITS FIRST PRINTING. 1834-01-07 c003 claimed this clause from the January reprint; this is the same ordinance four weeks earlier, adopted 4 December 1833, and it is the legal instrument under which every private wharf on the Chicago river was built. The terms are exact and the reconstruction can hold them: the riverfront lot owner may occupy the vacant ground BETWEEN HIS LOT AND THE WATER, provided EIGHTY FEET IS LEFT FOR A STREET, for wharfing only, on a fifteen-dollar annual lease running five years from 1 January 1834. So a wharf in this town is a leasehold on public ground with a statutory street behind it — which is a constraint on where wharf structures may stand, not merely a licence to build them. This printing is set more cleanly than the January one at the clause that matters; 1833-12-24 sets it cleaner still and is quoted at c005 of that issue for the eighty feet.

claims.notes: HARDSCRABBLE, PLACED BY ITS SURVEY DESCRIPTION. The corpus has the name of a place south-west of the town, and this notice is the only thing in it that says WHERE: fractional Section 29, Township 39 north, Range 14 east — a public-land description that resolves on the ground without any reading of local memory at all. Section 29 of T39N R14E is the south branch reach, and Beaubien is warning the town off it as private ground in December 1833. The subscriber is J. B. Beaubien (Jean Baptiste), who signs the Samuel Calhoun administration a week later (1833-12-17 c004) as Public Administrator for Cook county; the surname is also M. B. Beaubien's, appointed to the bridge committee in the same issue as this (c008), and the initials are what keep the two apart — see identity.json's standing rule that a shared surname with different initials never merges.
